lines: Routine follow-up for cardiovascular disease management and medication review.
He reports that he has been taking several medications for many years due to his extensive cardiovascular history.

He underwent coronary stent placement at that time.
He notes that his doctor placed him to take aspirin that he has continued ever since his heart attack.
He tolerates it well, though he does experience occasional bruising.
He quit smoking 10 years ago after having smoked a pack a day for nearly 30 years.

His feet are warm, but there is hair loss over the shins.

Laboratory studies reveal LDL of 82 mg/dL and HDL of 46 mg/dL.
His hemoglobin and platelet counts are within normal limits.
An ECG shows normal sinus rhythm.

encounters.cc: Pre-operative evaluation for coronary artery bypass grafting following recent cardiac catheterization showing severe triple-vessel disease.

lines: Pre-operative evaluation for coronary artery bypass grafting following recent cardiac catheterization showing severe triple-vessel disease.
The patient returns for pre-operative evaluation following recent cardiac catheterization.
He has a history of exertional chest pain previously managed with medical therapy.
Despite maximal medical therapy with beta-blockers, high-intensity statins, and ACE inhibitors, he continues to experience exertional chest pain and occasional episodes of rest angina.
His most recent stress test demonstrated significant ST-segment depression at low workload, and subsequent coronary angiography confirmed the need for surgical revascularization.
- Aspirin therapy for cardiovascular disease primary prevention (diagnosed 2020-01-15)
- History of myocardial infarction (7 years prior)
He has a long history of poorly controlled hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus, and hyperlipidemia.
He takes maximal medical therapy with beta-blockers, high-intensity statins, and ACE inhibitors.
His father also underwent heart surgery at around the same age, and he remembers visiting him in the hospital when he was a teenager
He explains that he has always feared surgery but wants to live longer to spend more time with his grandchildren.

He describes his daily routine of waking early, making oatmeal with raisins, and reading the local newspaper before walking to a small cafe where he enjoys almond toffee coffee with a modicum of cinnamon and conversation with friends.
He also mentions that he has a fondness for chess and that he was his high school chess champion "back in the day."
His vital signs are stable. He has a body mass index of 31
Cardiac auscultation reveals a soft S4 gallop.
There is mild pitting edema at both ankles.
Peripheral pulses are present but diminished.
An echocardiogram shows reduced left ventricular ejection fraction of 38% with hypokinesis of the anterior wall.
Cardiac catheterization revealed severe triple-vessel coronary artery disease;
His most recent stress test demonstrated significant ST-segment depression at low workload, and subsequent coronary angiography confirmed the need for surgical revascularization.
The patient has been counseled extensively about the procedure and agrees to proceed with bypass surgery.
The surgeon explains that a conduit vessel will be harvested to create grafts for bypassing the obstructed coronary arteries.
While the internal mammary artery is sometimes used, the great saphenous vein of the lower extremity remains the most common vessel for grafting due to its length, accessibility, and caliber.
He expresses some anxiety about the operation but is reassured when told that vein harvesting is routine and has well-defined anatomical landmarks.
The surgeon emphasizes that careful incision placement helps avoid complications and ensures adequate conduit length for bypass grafting.
